## [2]{.num} What open science is {.divider}

::: {.lines}
What it is, what drives it and what funders require
:::

::: {.notes}
**Time.** This section runs 6.5 minutes. The definition takes 1.5, the motives 1.5, the funder policy 1, the textbook picture 1 and the ecosystem around it 1.5.

**Where this fits.** The section sets out what open science asks for, why, and how funders turn it into requirements. It ends with the textbook picture of science and the ecosystem of identifiers, registries and standards that grew around it. The rest of the session tests what that picture assumes.
:::

## UNESCO's definition {.s2}

::: {.lines}
Practices that make scientific knowledge openly available, accessible and reusable for everyone

::: {.fragment}
and open the work of creating, evaluating and sharing it to society
:::
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.chips}
[Open scientific knowledge]{.chip} [Open infrastructures]{.chip} [Science communication]{.chip} [Open engagement of societal actors]{.chip} [Open dialogue with other knowledge systems]{.chip}
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
**Time.** 1.5 minutes.

**UNESCO 2021.**

- The UNESCO General Conference adopted the Recommendation on Open Science at its 41st session in Paris on November 23, 2021.
- The Recommendation defines open science as "an inclusive construct that combines various movements and practices aiming to make multilingual scientific knowledge openly available, accessible and reusable for everyone, to increase scientific collaborations and sharing of information for the benefits of science and society, and to open the processes of scientific knowledge creation, evaluation and communication to societal actors beyond the traditional scientific community." The slide shortens this.
- The chips are the five pillars the Recommendation names.
- It names four core values. They are quality and integrity, collective benefit, equity and fairness, and diversity and inclusiveness.

**Two halves.** The definition has two halves. The first half covers outputs, meaning knowledge that anyone can find, read and reuse. The second half covers who takes part in making it. It opens the creation, evaluation and communication of knowledge to people outside the traditional scientific community. Most discussion of open science stops at the first half. Sections 4 and 5 return to the second.
:::

## What motivates open science {.s2}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
### Epistemic

- Lets others check results
- Surfaces errors sooner
- Lets later studies reuse data
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
### Political and economic

- Makes funded research public
- Responds to subscription costs
- Gives funders something to audit
:::
:::

### What it includes

Open access, open data, open code, preregistration, open peer review, citizen science

::: {.notes}
**Time.** 1.5 minutes.

**Two sets of motives.**

- **Epistemic motives.**
  - Other researchers can check a result only if they can see the data and methods behind it.
  - More people looking means errors surface sooner.
  - Later studies can reuse data without collecting it again.
- **Political and economic motives.**
  - Public funders want the public to see what its money paid for.
  - Library subscription costs keep rising, and many institutions cannot afford them.
  - Open practices give funders and institutions something to audit.

**The practices on the slide lean one way or the other.** Open access leans political, and preregistration leans epistemic. Open data and open code serve both.

**Point.** The motives pull against each other. Different parts of the field answer to different motives.
:::

## The Tri-Agency data management policy {.s2}

| Requirement | Status |
|----------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------|
| Institutional RDM strategy | Each eligible institution had to post one by March 1, 2023 |
| Data management plan | Required at application for some funding opportunities, with more being added |
| Data deposit | Data, metadata and code behind publications, to be phased in with no dates yet |

::: {.notes}
**Time.** 1 minute.

**The policy.** Canada's three federal research funding agencies (CIHR, NSERC and SSHRC) issue the Tri-Agency Research Data Management Policy. The text is on the Government of Canada science site and was last modified on December 19, 2025.

- **Institutional strategies (section 3.1).** Each eligible institution creates a strategy, notifies the agencies and makes it publicly available. The deadline was March 1, 2023.
- **Data management plans (section 3.2).** The plan is required at application for the funding opportunities whose calls ask for one. The agencies continue to add the requirement to more calls, and no timeline for broader implementation has been finalized.
- **Data deposit (section 3.3).** Recipients must deposit the data, metadata and code that directly support the conclusions of journal publications and pre-prints. The agencies are phasing this in after reviewing institutional strategies and have given no dates. CIHR recipients have been subject to a narrower deposit requirement since January 1, 2008.

**Point.** Funders turn the political motive into a requirement.

**What to stress.** The deposit requirement is not yet in force for most grants. Do not tell the class otherwise.

**Ask.** Take one show of hands on who expects to read, write or review one of these documents in a first job.
:::

## The textbook picture {.s2}

::: {.flow}
<span class="step">Question</span><span class="arrow">→</span><span class="step">Hypothesis</span><span class="arrow">→</span><span class="step">Experiment</span><span class="arrow">→</span><span class="step">Data</span><span class="arrow">→</span><span class="step">Paper</span>
:::

::: {.fragment}
### Open science adds

::: {.chips}
[Share the data]{.chip .hl} [Share the code]{.chip .hl} [Share the paper]{.chip .hl}
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
**Time.** 1 minute.

**The picture.** This is the version of science most of us learned in school. A scientist asks a question, forms a hypothesis, runs an experiment, collects data and writes a paper.

**What open science adds.** In this picture, open science extends the end of the line. After the paper, the scientist shares the data, the code and the paper itself.

**What the picture assumes.** It treats sharing as one more step at the end. It assumes one kind of science, one scientist, data that arrive as a byproduct, and release as the goal.

**Plant it.** Everything after this slide tests what the picture assumes. Sections 3, 4 and 5 take its assumptions about data, access, infrastructure, method and labour in turn. The closing table in section 5 lists all six.
:::

## The ecosystem around a paper {.s2}

```{=html}
<div class="eco">
  <div class="eco-col">
    <div class="node left"><img class="logo" src="img/orcid.svg" alt="ORCID logo"><div><b>Authors</b><span>An ORCID iD identifies each person</span></div></div>
    <div class="node left"><img class="logo" src="img/ror.svg" alt="ROR logo"><div><b>Institutions</b><span>A ROR ID identifies each affiliation</span></div></div>
    <div class="node left"><span class="logo txt">CRediT</span><div><b>Contributions</b><span>14 roles say what each author did</span></div></div>
  </div>
  <div class="hub">
    <img class="logo" src="img/crossref.svg" alt="Crossref logo">
    <b>The paper</b>
    <span>Its DOI is registered with Crossref</span>
  </div>
  <div class="eco-col">
    <div class="node right"><img class="logo" src="img/doi.svg" alt="DOI logo"><div><b>Funding</b><span>A grant DOI ties the paper to its grant</span></div></div>
    <div class="node right"><img class="logo" src="img/osf.svg" alt="OSF logo"><div><b>Plan</b><span>A registration records the plan before data collection</span></div></div>
    <div class="node right"><img class="logo" src="img/datacite.svg" alt="DataCite logo"><div><b>Data</b><span>A DataCite DOI points to the deposited dataset</span></div></div>
  </div>
</div>
<div class="fragment eco-bar">
  <span class="logo txt">OpenAlex</span>
  <span>indexes these records and the links between them in one free, open catalogue. Each link depends on someone supplying the identifier.</span>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
**Time.** 1.5 minutes.

**Run it.** The paper sits in the middle. Read each node on the left, then each on the right, by what it does for the paper. Press the arrow key once to bring up OpenAlex and the last sentence.

**How the pieces relate.** Each identifier is a key. A paper's record carries the keys of everything around it, and other systems follow those keys to build the links. Each node is run by a different organization.

- **Authors.** ORCID is a nonprofit funded by member fees. It gives researchers a persistent identifier, free of charge.
- **Institutions.** ROR is a community-led registry of open identifiers for research organizations. California Digital Library, Crossref and DataCite operate it, and the data are CC0.
- **Contributions.** CRediT is the Contributor Roles Taxonomy. It has 14 roles, such as data curation and software, and it is published as ANSI/NISO Z39.104-2022 under a CC BY 4.0 licence.
- **The paper.** Crossref and DataCite are the two registration agencies on the slide. Crossref registers the DOI for the paper.
- **Funding.** Crossref describes grant DOIs that funders register with Crossref or DataCite, so that outputs link to the grant behind them. The Crossref page consulted for this deck described a pilot, so check its current status before you say it is in routine use. **To add.** The slide reads "open grants" as grant identifiers. If you meant funders publishing the proposals themselves, change the node.
- **Plan.** The Center for Open Science defines preregistration as "specifying your research plan in advance of your study and submitting it to a registry." Registered reports go further. Peer review happens before data collection, and accepted protocols get in-principle acceptance. COS says over 300 journals use the format, and accepted protocols can be registered on the OSF Registry.
- **Data.** A repository such as Zenodo registers a DOI for each deposit through DataCite.
- **OpenAlex.** A free and open catalogue of the world's research, run by a small nonprofit team, with CC0 data.

**Not on the slide.** Open access, preprints, open protocols, FAIR metadata, licences and data management plans also grew up around the picture. Say that the slide is a sample.

**Point.** The links exist only if someone supplies the identifiers and fills in the fields. The textbook picture has no step for that work, and section 5 returns to it.

**Addresses.** cos.io/initiatives/registered-reports, credit.niso.org, orcid.org, ror.org, openalex.org and crossref.org. Logos come from Academicons, which is licensed under the SIL OFL 1.1. CRediT and OpenAlex have no icon in that set, so they appear as text.
:::
